title: What We Choose to Keep
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 39 of 40
content:
We found the Death Eater robes in a trunk beneath three generations of Prince family linens.

It was exactly the sort of absurdity Spinner's End specialized in.

A hand-embroidered tablecloth. Two moth-eaten blankets. A stack of yellowed letters tied with green ribbon. Then, beneath them, folded with unbearable neatness, black fabric from a life Severus had spent years trying to outlive.

He stared into the trunk.

I sat back on my heels.

We had been clearing the upstairs room for almost an hour. The laboratory was finished, his Hogwarts schedule had settled, and the house had finally reached the stage where renovation required decisions about objects rather than walls.

Objects were worse.

Walls did not remember you.

“What do you want to do with them?” I asked.

His jaw tightened.

“I am considering whether Incendio would damage the floorboards.”

“Practical.”

“I strive for consistency.”

He did not reach for his wand.

I did not reach for the robes.

That had become one of the most important things I knew how to do with Severus: leave space around a choice without abandoning him inside it.

He lifted the green-ribboned letters first.

“My mother's.”

“To whom?”

“My grandmother, mostly.”

“Do you want to read them?”

“No.”

A beat.

“Not today,” he corrected.

I nodded.

We had three boxes on the floor.

KEEP.

ARCHIVE.

DESTROY.

The labels had been my idea. Severus had mocked them for being simplistic, then charmed the lettering so it could not smudge.

The letters went into ARCHIVE.

The tablecloth went into KEEP after Severus admitted, with visible resentment, that his mother had embroidered it herself.

A cracked silver photograph frame went into KEEP too. The picture inside showed a much younger Eileen Prince before marriage, dark-haired and unsmiling in school robes. Severus touched the edge of the image once.

“My mother was not kind,” he said.

I waited.

“Nor was she uniformly cruel.”

“People rarely cooperate with categories.”

“No. Inconvenient of them.”

He set the frame carefully into the box.

The Death Eater robes remained in the trunk.

“What about those?” I asked eventually.

His eyes went flat.

“They are evidence.”

“Of what?”

“My stupidity.”

“You have other evidence.”

His mouth twitched despite himself.

“Abundant evidence,” I added.

“Thank you.”

“Any time.”

He looked back at the robes.

“Destroying them feels theatrical.”

“Keeping them could be theatrical too.”

His gaze shifted toward me.

“Explain.”

“People keep ugly relics because they think suffering deserves a museum. Sometimes it does. Sometimes it becomes another way to kneel in front of the past.”

He was silent.

I had learned not to soften every difficult statement after saying it. Severus respected the full weight of words. He could forgive clumsiness more readily than cowardice.

“I don't know which this is for you,” I said. “That's why I'm asking.”

He reached into the trunk.

The robes came free with a whisper of old fabric.

For a moment he held them against the light.

They were smaller than I expected.

That startled me more than anything.

Not tiny. Not child-sized. But narrow through the shoulders, cut for a younger man who had not yet grown into the severe shape I knew. They made his recruitment suddenly physical. There had been a body inside this cloth. A young adult body. Angry, ambitious, humiliated, frightened, cruel, talented, and convinced belonging to something powerful might make the world stop making him feel small.

It did not make him innocent.

It made the mistake human-sized.

Severus saw where I was looking.

“I was twenty-one when I turned spy,” he said.

“I know.”

“I joined before that.”

“I know.”

“You are doing that thing.”

“What thing?”

“Looking at me as though chronology is an emotion.”

I exhaled through my nose. “I was thinking you were young.”

His expression hardened. “Old enough.”

“Yes.”

The hardness faltered.

I did not argue him out of responsibility. He did not force me to condemn the younger version of him until there was nothing left to understand.

That was the compromise we had built over months.

He lowered the robes.

“I do not want them in the house.”

“Then they don't stay in the house.”

“I do not want to sell them, donate them to some morbid collection, or permit a historian to turn them into a footnote about redemption.”

“Then don't.”

His wand appeared in his hand.

This time he moved without hesitation.

We took the robes outside.

The narrow yard behind Spinner's End was damp from morning rain. The new laboratory windows reflected a colorless sky. Severus laid the fabric inside an old iron brazier that had once held coal.

He did not make a speech.

Neither did I.

“Incendio.”

Fire caught along the hem.

The black cloth curled inward, orange eating through old wool. A silver fastening fell loose and struck the metal basin with a sharp ping.

Severus watched until the last recognizable fold collapsed.

Then he extinguished the remains.

“That was less satisfying than fiction suggests,” he said.

“Most symbolic acts probably are.”

“Entirely inadequate.”

“Want me to clap?”

“No.”

“Cry?”

“Certainly not.”

“Say something about rising from ashes?”

“If you do, I will put you in the brazier.”

I smiled.

His shoulder touched mine.

We stood there another minute anyway.

Back upstairs, the clearing became easier.

We found school essays Severus had written at fifteen, covered in red corrections from Slughorn and even denser black notes he had added later to correct the corrections. We found a broken quill, a small collection of potion bottle stoppers, three books in French, one in German, and a Muggle chemistry text so outdated that I laughed until Severus threatened to confiscate my lungs.

We found a scarf.

Red and gold.

Neither of us spoke.

The fabric was faded almost to brown at the edges.

He touched it as if it might burn.

“Lily's?” I asked.

“No.”

I waited.

“Mine.”

I stared.

He looked murderous.

“You owned a Gryffindor scarf?”

“It was acquired under circumstances that are none of your concern.”

“Severus.”

“No.”

“Did she give it to you?”

“No.”

“Did you steal it?”

His silence answered too much.

I sat down hard on the floor and laughed.

“I was eleven,” he snapped.

That made it worse.

Tears came to my eyes.

“Stop.”

“I can't.”

“You are intolerable.”

“You stole Lily Evans's Gryffindor scarf?”

“I returned it.”

“You are holding it.”

“A different scarf.”

I laughed harder.

For one glorious minute, Severus Snape—former spy, former Death Eater, former Headmaster, terror of generations of schoolchildren—was reduced to arguing that there had apparently been two scarves and only one had been stolen.

When I finally recovered, he was sitting against the opposite wall with the expression of a man reconsidering every decision that had led to romance.

“What box?” I asked.

He looked down at the scarf.

His thumb moved over the old wool.

“Keep.”

I nodded.

No jealousy arrived.

No ache of competition.

Just tenderness for the ridiculous eleven-year-old who had wanted something bright enough to steal it.

Severus placed the scarf in the box beside his mother's tablecloth.

Then he picked up the annotated Potions textbook.

“That stays,” I said.

“I had not asked.”

“You were thinking too loudly.”

“It is historically incriminating.”

“It is also brilliant.”

“Parts of it are adolescent nonsense.”

“So are parts of everyone.”

He looked at the book for a long time.

Then he set it in KEEP.

By evening, the room was nearly empty.

Three boxes remained.

KEEP was the fullest.

ARCHIVE held documents that mattered but did not need to live at the center of daily life.

DESTROY contained surprisingly little.

I thought about that as we sat on the floor eating takeaway from paper cartons because neither of us had the energy to cook.

Healing, I had once imagined, meant throwing away enough of the past that the future had room.

Severus had taught me something stranger.

Sometimes room was made by deciding what an object was allowed to mean.

A scarf could be a memory without being a shrine.

A textbook could contain cruelty and genius on adjacent pages.

A family photograph could survive without pretending the family had been happy.

A house could remember and still change.

Severus nudged my knee with his.

“You are staring.”

“Thinking.”

“Dangerous.”

“About keeping you.”

His eyes narrowed.

“I am not an object to be sorted into one of your boxes.”

“Good. You'd exceed the weight limit.”

He took my carton away.

“Hey.”

“Consequences.”

I leaned over and stole it back.

He let me.

That went in KEEP too.
